title: Martin v. Wilks
lead: Employment consent decrees resolved one set of discrimination claims, but white firefighters who were not parties later asserted independent rights against promotions implementing those decrees.

actors.name: Wilks and other white firefighters
actors.role: Plaintiffs in the later discrimination action

actors.name: City of Birmingham and Jefferson County Personnel Board

proceedings: Earlier discrimination litigation produced consent decrees.
District court dismissed the later suit after finding promotions pursuant to the decrees.
Eleventh Circuit reversed; Supreme Court affirmed 5–4.
limits: The Court did not determine promotion illegality, candidate qualifications, or wholesale invalidity of the decrees. Congress separately qualified employment-decree challenges in 1991 under 42 U.S.C. § 2000e-2(n).

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: Employment discrimination litigation produces negotiated remedies
sections.cue: Other firefighters object without becoming decree parties
paragraphs: Beginning in 1974, black individuals, an NAACP branch, and the United States challenged Birmingham’s and the Jefferson County Personnel Board’s employment practices under Title VII and other federal law. The litigation eventually produced consent decrees with goals for hiring black firefighters and promoting black employees.

The Birmingham Firefighters Association appeared as an amicus and objected at the fairness hearing. It and two members later sought intervention, which was denied as untimely. Separately, seven white firefighters failed to obtain an injunction against approval. In reviewing the intervention denial, the Eleventh Circuit indicated that independent discrimination claims remained available. These proceedings were distinct from the later Wilks group’s action.

sections.title: Wilks and other nonparties challenge later promotions
sections.cue: The district court treats decree compliance as dispositive
paragraphs: Wilks and other white firefighters sued the City and Board, alleging that race denied them promotions in favor of less-qualified black applicants. Black firefighters and other decree beneficiaries intervened in defense. The qualifications and unlawful-treatment assertions were allegations, not Supreme Court findings.

The City and Board answered that the decisions implemented the decrees. The district court tried the action under a framework shielding decree-required promotions and dismissed after finding the decisions made pursuant to the decrees. The Eleventh Circuit reversed, concluding that nonparties’ claims could not be barred simply because the decisions implemented earlier judgments. Martin and other decree defenders, along with petitions associated with the City and Board, sought Supreme Court review.

sections.title: The majority puts the burden on those seeking a binding judgment
sections.cue: Opportunity to intervene does not itself surrender an independent right
paragraphs: Chief Justice Rehnquist, joined by Justices White, O’Connor, Scalia, and Kennedy, began with the ordinary rule that an in personam judgment does not bind a nonparty. A hearing on someone else’s claims, however extensive or important, does not itself adjudicate an outsider’s independent rights. Appropriate representation and special statutory proceedings can supply recognized exceptions, but mere knowledge and an opportunity to intervene do not.

Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 24 allowed intervention rather than generally requiring it. Amicus participation or a chance to object was not equivalent to party status. Litigants seeking to bind affected people ordinarily had to secure joinder under the applicable rules. Rule 19 addressed who should be included and how to proceed if joinder was impossible; the Court did not say every case must stop whenever every practically affected person was absent.

Those negotiating relief knew what they sought and were better placed to identify whom they wished to bind. A mandatory-intervention rule instead required outsiders to monitor litigation, predict settlement effects, and guess when their rights were threatened. Later disputes about notice and opportunity would shift, rather than remove, costs. Settlement finality mattered, but parties could not purchase it by settling claims they did not own.

Defendants remained free to contest the later claims on the merits. Simply describing decree compliance as substantive justification rather than preclusion did not cure a rule that defeated an otherwise valid claim solely through another person’s judgment.

sections.title: Stevens disputes the majority’s description of the trial
sections.cue: The dissent treats compliance as lawful remedial conduct
paragraphs: Justice Stevens, joined by Justices Brennan, Marshall, and Blackmun, agreed with the general nonparty rule but thought it misapplied. In his account, extensive earlier litigation exposed unlawful employment practices, and the decrees established a lawful remedial program. The later district court had heard and rejected the white firefighters’ claims on their merits.

He distinguished preclusion from the legal and practical consequences of obeying a court order. Qualifications findings, the limited remedies, and the defendants’ duty to comply could justify decisions without denying outsiders every right to sue. His reading of the Board’s record also found evidence missing even for an initial discrimination showing. These were dissenting evaluations, not findings adopted by the majority.
Stevens regarded the majority’s mandatory-intervention discussion as unnecessary and would vacate the Eleventh Circuit and remand under his merits-based understanding.

sections.title: The independent claims return for further proceedings
sections.cue: Later legislation narrows some employment-decree challenges
paragraphs: On June 12, 1989, the Supreme Court affirmed the Eleventh Circuit’s reversal. Because the erroneous decree-based framework could affect merits findings, the firefighters’ independent claims required further consideration. The Court awarded no promotions and did not adjudge black candidates unqualified, declare the challenged decisions discriminatory, or invalidate every decree provision.

In 1991 Congress added 42 U.S.C. § 2000e-2(n). For specified practices implementing and within discrimination judgments or orders, it restricts challenges by people given actual notice and a reasonable objection opportunity or adequately represented in a prior challenge on the same grounds and similar facts, subject to qualifications. It preserves due process and exceptions including fraud, collusion, transparent invalidity, and absence of subject-matter jurisdiction. That separate enactment limits using Martin alone as a complete account of employment-decree law.

sources.pinpoint: 490 U.S. at 768–769; later statutory qualification in reviewed brief, 42 U.S.C. § 2000e-2(n)
